name: Herbicide injury — clomazone-type bleaching
summary: An exposure-confirmed hemp differential for Group 13 clomazone injury. Compatible new-growth bleaching is highly nonspecific: a clomazone label requires a temporally and spatially plausible soil-carryover, pre-emergence, or vapor-drift pathway, ideally strengthened by records or residue analysis.
affectedParts: older foliage later in sustained injury
indicators: The youngest expanding leaves or shoot tips become pale green, pale yellow, or nearly white while older pre-exposure foliage may initially retain more green pigment

Pigment loss can be interveinal, marginal, patchy, or nearly complete rather than following a single Cannabis-specific shape; occasional pink-to-purple margins may occur in sensitive non-Cannabis plants
Affected tissue may remain bleached and growth-reduced, advance to necrosis under severe exposure, or be followed by normally green new growth after a limited exposure
Several Cannabis plants share a boundary, downwind, previous-crop, treated-soil, bed, container-lot, equipment, or irrigation-source pattern rather than a random single-leaf pattern
Susceptible weeds or other plant species near the same field edge may show compatible pigment loss, strengthening a vapor-drift hypothesis without proving the active ingredient
A documented commercial hemp field case linked clomazone soil carryover to bleaching of newly formed tissue and nonrecovery
A controlled pre-emergence greenhouse screen found severe stand, height, and biomass reductions in Felina 32 hemp at the tested clomazone rate, establishing hemp sensitivity under those conditions
exclusions: No plausible clomazone or related pigment-inhibitor source, timing, route, field history, neighboring application, equipment pathway, or residue evidence can be established
Iron, sulfur, manganese, root-zone pH, EC, water status, or tissue results explain the leaf-age and canopy pattern better
Bleaching is restricted to the most light-exposed canopy surface or lamp footprint and measured irradiance or heat history supports photooxidative injury
Stable sectoral or clone-recurrent variegation persists without an exposure gradient, growth suppression, or injury progression
Magnification finds broad mites, hemp russet mites, thrips, feeding scars, eggs, cast skins, or webbing linked to the affected tissue
Discrete lesions, surface growth, ooze, vascular discoloration, root/crown disease, or validated pathogen testing supports an infectious cause
Rapid droplet-shaped scorch, bronzing, or near-immediate necrosis fits a contact or PPO-inhibitor exposure better than carotenoid-inhibitor bleaching
Color loss disappears under neutral calibrated lighting or is attributable to clipping, white balance, overexposure, compression, or infrared imaging

progression.description: A soil, pre-emergence, carryover, contaminated-equipment, irrigation, or off-target vapor pathway precedes symptoms; preserve records before altering the site.
New shoot tips and expanding leaves lose pigment first, ranging from pale green or yellow to nearly white while older foliage may remain greener.
Limited exposure may be followed by green new growth above older bleached leaves; sustained or severe injury can suppress growth and extend pigment loss.
Severely bleached tissue can become necrotic, and young plants exposed through soil may be more severely affected than established plants receiving limited drift.
The North Carolina carryover case did not recover, but institutional sources describe recovery after lighter exposure; outcome cannot be inferred from one frame.

lookAlikes: Broad mite or hemp russet mite injury
confirmation: Capture neutral-color whole-area video plus matched upper, middle, and lower canopy stills, close-ups of both leaf surfaces, and unaffected comparison plants before any correction.

Map affected and unaffected Cannabis plants against field edges, wind direction, previous-crop rows, treated soil, bed or container lots, irrigation zones, traffic routes, and application or transplant dates.
Photograph susceptible weeds and other plant species along affected and unaffected edges; shared bleaching supports an exposure plume but does not identify clomazone.

Reconstruct product, active ingredient, rate, formulation, application, weather, soil, prior-crop restriction, equipment-cleanout, substrate, and water-treatment records with a qualified crop professional.

Preserve plant, soil, water, and product samples under an accredited laboratory chain of custody when residue analysis is appropriate; interpret nondetection with sampling time, analyte, matrix, and method limits.
Measure root-zone pH, EC, moisture, and temperature and obtain plant tissue analysis where appropriate to test nutrient and root-zone alternatives.
Inspect growing tips with magnification and submit plant-linked tissue for pathogen testing when pest or infectious differentials remain plausible.
Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, non-Cannabis, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, and exposure-unlinked samples out of the confirmed clomazone class and automated training.
immediateActions: Stop further suspected exposure without disturbing evidence; preserve labels, spray and field records, weather data, equipment-cleanout history, and representative samples.
Segregate suspect plant lots and prevent contaminated soil, substrate, water, tools, or equipment from moving into unaffected production areas.
Do not apply speculative nutrients, pesticides, or flushing treatments before documenting the pre-correction pattern and root-zone measurements.
correctivePlan: Base any response on the confirmed exposure route, residue context, plant stage, local pesticide law, and qualified agronomic guidance; this diagnostic record does not recommend herbicide use or a universal remediation.
Track the same plants and fixed viewpoints through later growth, recording whether green tissue resumes, bleaching progresses, necrosis develops, or plants fail to recover.
Investigate nutrient, light, pest, and pathogen alternatives concurrently when exposure evidence is incomplete or mixed.
prevention: Maintain complete pesticide, crop-rotation, field, substrate, water, and equipment-cleanout records and review legally applicable plant-back restrictions before hemp establishment.
Use drift-reduction, buffer, application-timing, and equipment-segregation practices required by the product label and local regulations.
Record baseline imagery and unaffected comparison areas so a later boundary or plume pattern can be evaluated.
warnings: Bleached Cannabis tissue cannot identify clomazone, dose, formulation, route, or legal source from appearance alone; photo/video confidence is capped at 0.20.
The controlled clomazone experiment tested one hemp cultivar, one greenhouse soil system, and one pre-emergence rate; its quantitative injury is not a universal Cannabis threshold.
The field nonrecovery case and institutional lighter-exposure recovery guidance describe different exposure contexts and should not be collapsed into a deterministic prognosis.
The two licensed NC State images show grape and pokeweed, not Cannabis; they are transfer references for color and field-edge context only and are excluded from Cannabis training and evaluation.
No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis clomazone progression image or verified diagnostic video was located for this batch.
This profile is an injury-identification differential, not a pesticide recommendation or substitute for label, regulatory, laboratory, or professional advice.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.

sources.title: Evaluating herbicide tolerance of industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.)
sources.publisher: Wiley on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America
supportedClaims: In a randomized greenhouse pre-emergence screen using Cannabis sativa cultivar Felina 32, clomazone at 1.4 kg active ingredient per hectare produced only two surviving plants per pot, 8 cm mean plant height, and 0.6 g mean biomass at eight weeks, versus seven plants, 49 cm, and 13.5 g in the untreated check.

Across the greenhouse screen, clomazone was among treatments that reduced stand count 43–71%, height 47–84%, and biomass 73–96% relative to the untreated check; the paper groups clomazone and norflurazon as highly injurious pigment inhibitors.

Clomazone was screened pre-emergence in the greenhouse but was not advanced into the field study, so the experiment supports severe hemp sensitivity under its tested rate and conditions rather than a universal field threshold or a visual diagnosis.
The authors reported that hemp responses varied across environments, years, and cultivars for tested herbicides and called for corroboration before commercial recommendations.

sources.title: Herbicide Damage Symptoms on Hemp
sources.organization: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, UC Weed Science
sources.publisher: Regents of the University of California
supportedClaims: The institutional hemp demonstration exposed plants to herbicides used near hemp production to document injury expected from specific active ingredients or related modes of action.

Its clomazone example identifies carotenoid-biosynthesis inhibition: bleaching ranges from yellow to almost pure white, begins in newly formed tissue, may progress to older tissue as existing carotenoids turn over, and can advance to necrosis.

The guide distinguishes potentially dramatic but rarely lethal established-plant drift injury from more damaging soil-carryover injury to seedlings or young transplants; these are contextual patterns, not dose-independent outcome guarantees.

The source PDF contains mixed herbicide-treatment photographs without a verified reusable asset license or panel-level training labels, so those figures are citation evidence only and are not indexed as reusable media.

sources.title: Carotenoid Pigments
supportedClaims: Carotenoid-pigment-inhibitor injury can produce white, pale-yellow, or pale-green new shoot tips and leaves, occasional pink-to-purple margins, reduced growth, and later necrosis; resumed green growth can appear above older bleached foliage in less-sensitive plants.

The guide identifies clomazone as a soil-absorbed Group 13 pigment inhibitor with high vapor-drift potential and recommends inspecting susceptible weeds and other plants along field edges for a shared exposure pattern.

Severe iron deficiency, bleaching infections, contact-herbicide injury, PPO-inhibitor bronzing, air pollution, and insect-growth-regulator exposure can overlap visually and require contextual exclusion.
The grape and pokeweed photographs are explicitly credited to J. Neal under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, but they are non-Cannabis transfer references and do not establish clomazone injury in hemp.

media.caption: NC State Extension clomazone vapor-drift reference on grape. It illustrates near-white pigment loss with retained green vein regions, but it is not a Cannabis sample and does not establish a universal clomazone pattern.

useLimitations: Non-Cannabis transfer reference; do not use it to label Cannabis condition, severity, dose, route, progression, or recovery.
One close-up lacks whole-field distribution, application history, temporal sequence, unaffected comparison, and laboratory residue linkage.
The CC BY-NC-SA license restricts reuse to noncommercial purposes and requires adaptations to use the same license; automated training is prohibited by dataset policy.
Retained green vein regions and white margins are not clomazone-specific and can overlap micronutrient, pathogen, light, or imaging effects.

media.severity: substantial pigment loss on one grape leaf; not transferable to Cannabis
